system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-09-01 15:29:00 to 2184-09-09 15:11:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted after experiencing a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure, likely due to four days of missed antiepileptic medications after leaving rehab against medical advice. He presented with hypoglycemia (glucose 44) and transient hypotension, both managed with dextrose and IV fluids. CT scans showed no acute intracranial or cervical spine abnormalities. He was loaded with IV levetiracetam and restarted on oral seizure medications, remaining seizure-free during admission. Hypotension recurred post-dialysis but resolved with cautious fluid administration. A skin swab near his femoral dialysis catheter grew staph and VRE, prompting a short course of vancomycin, though blood cultures remained negative and infection was not confirmed. An incidental enlarged thyroid with calcifications was noted on imaging; TSH was normal, and outpatient ultrasound was recommended. The patient was medically stable by discharge, alert, ambulating with a walker, and deemed competent to reside in a hotel while securing independent housing. He was discharged on updated medications with clear instructions for dialysis attendance, weight monitoring, and neurology and primary care follow-up.
problems: Generalized convulsive epilepsy, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Other and unspecified infection due to central venous catheter
Personal history of transient ischemic attack (TIA), and cerebral infarction without residual deficits
Open wound of forehead, without mention of complication
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health
Kidney dialysis as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, now
with fever and hypotension.

STUDY:  Portable upright frontal chest radiograph.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  The heart size is at the upper limits of normal, likely exaggerated
by technique.  The mediastinal contours demonstrate calcified atherosclerotic
disease of the aortic knob.  The hilar contours are normal.  The lungs are
clear.  There is no pleural effusion or pneumothorax.  The osseous structures
demonstrate multiple old right posterior rib fractures.

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary process.

PROCEDURE:  Removal of tunneled left common femoral vein hemodialysis
catheter.

HISTORY:  ___ man with end-stage renal disease with longstanding
left-sided tunneled femoral HD catheter.  The patient is bacteremic and
requires line removal.

ANESTHESIA:  10 mL of 1% lidocaine was administered to the skin along the
catheter tunnel tract.

RADIOLOGIST:  Dr. ___ performed the procedure.  Dr. ___, the
attending radiologist supervised the procedure.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  Informed verbal consent was obtained outlining the
risks and benefits of the procedure involved.  Following this the patient was
brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the imaging table.  The
existing left groin catheter and surrounding catheter were prepped and draped
in the usual sterile fashion.  A preprocedure huddle and timeout were
performed as per ___ protocol. 

10 mLs of 1% lidocaine was administered to the tissues around the catheter
tract.  Blunt dissection was performed around the catheter cuff and the line
was removed with gentle traction in its entirety.  The tip was sent for
culture and sensitivity.  Manual pressure was applied to the venotomy and skin
exit site for 15 minutes.  Good hemostasis was achieved and a sterile dressing
was applied.  There were no early complications.  The patient tolerated the
procedure well.

IMPRESSION:  Uncomplicated removal of left-sided tunneled hemodialysis
catheter via the left common femoral vein access point.  The catheter tip was
sent for culture and sensitivity.  There was good hemostasis and a sterile
dressing was applied.

The staff radiologist has reviewed the images and the report.

MEDICAL HISTORY:  ___ man with end-stage renal disease, on
hemodialysis.  A groin HD line was pulled out a few days ago for MRSA
bacteremia and for line holiday.  Today, the patient presents for placement of
a new tunneled HD catheter.

CLINICIANS:  Dr. ___ and Dr. ___.  Dr. ___ attending
radiologist, was present and supervising throughout.

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
50 mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of Versed throughout the total intraservice time
of 20 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored.  Local anesthesia with 1% lidocaine and 1% lidocaine
with epinephrine.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  An informed written consent was obtained after
explaining the procedure, benefits, alternatives and risks involved.  The
patient was brought to angiography suite and an ultrasound examination of the
neck was performed prior to the procedure; it demonstrated bilateral
occlusions of the internal jugular veins.  However, the external jugular veins
were patent on both sides and there was evidence of multiple collateral veins
in the neck.  A decision was made to attempt placement of an external jugular
venous catheter on the right side.  The right side of the neck and upper chest
were prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.  Preprocedure huddle and
timeout were performed as per ___ protocol.

Under ultrasound guidance with hard copy images on file, access was obtained
into a patent right external jugular vein with a micropuncture set.  However,
the guidewire could not be advanced past the right brachiocephalic vein. Then,
a venogram was performed by contrast injection through the micropuncture
sheath, which demonstrated complete occlusion of the right brachiocephalic
vein with extensive collateral formation.  Attempts to cross the obstruction
with guidewire were unsuccessful.  Therefore, the procedure was abandoned and
a decision was made to attempt placement of the line on the left side.  The
micropuncture sheath was removed and hemostasis was achieved with digital
compression.  A sterile dressing was applied.

Next, the left side of the neck and upper chest were prepped and draped in the
usual sterile fashion.  Access was obtained into a patent left external
jugular vein with a micropuncture set under ultrasound guidance.  From this
access, the guidewire could be easily advanced into the right atrium.  After
taking appropriate measurements, the 0.035 ___ wire was advanced into IVC
under fluoroscopic control using a Kumpe catheter.  Then, attention was
directed to tunneling the HD catheter.  A small skin incision was made over
the left upper chest.  A 27 cm tip-to-cuff hemodialysis catheter was tunneled
through from the left upper chest and brought out at the venotomy site. 
Because of the acute angulation at left brachiocephalic and SVC junction, the
guidewire was exchanged for a super stiff Amplatz wire through the Kumpe
catheter.  The soft tissue tract was then dilated over the wire.  A peel-away
sheath was placed and the inner dilator as well as the guidewire were removed.
The catheter was placed through the peel-away sheath and tip advanced into the
right atrium.  The peel-away sheath was then removed.  Both ports of the
catheter were easily aspirated and flushed.  A fluoroscopic spot chest film
was obtained and stored digitally.  The catheter was secured to the skin with
0 silk sutures and venotomy site closed with ___ Vicryl suture.  Sterile
dressings were applied.  Patient tolerated the procedure well and there were
no immediate complications.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Ultrasound examination demonstrated complete occlusion of both internal
jugular veins with patent external jugular veins bilaterally and extensive
collateral formation in the neck.
2.  Attempt to place a HD catheter via right external jugular venous access
was unsuccessful as there was complete occlusion of the right brachiocephalic
vein which was confirmed by a venogram.
3.  Successful ultrasound and fluoroscopically guided placement of a 27 cm
tip-to-cuff tunneled hemodialysis catheter via left external jugular venous
access with the tip of the catheter terminating in the right atrium.  The line
is ready for use.

HISTORY:  Fluctuant left groin at site of prior hemodialysis catheter. 
Evaluate for underlying fluid collection or abscess.

COMPARISON:  CT torso ___.

TARGETED LEFT LOWER EXTREMITY ULTRASOUND
Focused sonographic evaluation in the left groin was performed demonstrating
normal appearance to the greater saphenous vein, common femoral vein, and
common femoral artery.  No deep fluid collections were noted.  A trace amount
of free fluid is noted within the subcutaneous tissues in immediate vicinity
to a linear hypoechoic tract which extends to the common femoral vein from the
skin surface related to the prior HD catheter.  No internal vascular flow is
noted within the tract confirming nonpatency.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No deep fluid collections identified in the left groin.

2.  Minimal amount of superficial subcutaneous fluid noted in the immediate
vicinity of the prior HD catheter tract site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You came in from dialysis with a fever and low blood pressure. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I felt weak and dizzy at dialysis. They said I had a fever and my blood pressure dropped. I didn’t feel that sick, just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve started you on antibiotics because we think your dialysis line might be infected. We also put in a temporary line in your other groin to help with blood pressure support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had problems with that line before. It’s been draining a bit, even after they changed it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s concerning. We’re waiting on blood cultures, but if the line is infected, we’ll likely need to remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I still be able to get dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Once we remove the infected line, you’ll have a short break from dialysis—what we call a 'line holiday'—until we place a new one safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds okay. But will I be okay without dialysis for a few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable for now, so you don’t need urgent dialysis. We’ll monitor your fluid and electrolytes closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your first blood culture didn’t grow anything, which is good, but we’re still concerned. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another blood culture came back negative. That’s reassuring, but we’re still seeing signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they sure it’s the line? I feel a bit better today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not 100% sure yet, but your line has been problematic. We’re planning to remove it today to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just removed your tunneled dialysis line. The tip was sent for culture. We’ll know more in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your line tip grew Staph aureus. That confirms the infection. It’s resistant to some antibiotics, so we’re continuing vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that MRSA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s MRSA. That’s why we’re using vancomycin. You’ll need it for several weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get it here the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you’ll go home and get it during your dialysis sessions. We’ll coordinate with your dialysis center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s better than staying here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your next blood culture was negative. That’s a great sign—means the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure is more stable, you’re not spiking fevers, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another negative blood culture. That’s three in a row—very encouraging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I get a new dialysis line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We usually wait about a week after clearing the infection. We’re planning for later this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your repeat blood cultures are negative. That means the MRSA is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I can get my new line soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled for tomorrow. We’ll place it in your neck this time, not the groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the neck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It has better blood flow and lower infection risk. Your groin veins are also partly blocked, so neck is safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reviewing imaging of your neck veins today to plan for tomorrow’s procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a chance it won’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a small chance, but we’ll use ultrasound and X-ray guidance. We’re confident we can place it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your new tunneled dialysis line was placed successfully this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely in a day or two. You’ll need one more dialysis session here to make sure everything works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on vancomycin for a while. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We check your levels weekly to make sure it’s safe. Your kidney function also affects dosing, so we adjust for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a heart ultrasound yesterday. It showed your heart function is a bit worse than before, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Infections can stress the heart. We’re holding your blood pressure medication for now to avoid low pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on lisinopril. Is that stopped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered the dose to 2.5 mg. We’ll keep it low until your heart function is reassessed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your old groin site. There’s a little fluid, but no abscess. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s healing well. Just keep the area clean and watch for redness or drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most stay the same. We stopped lanthanum because we’re using other phosphate binders now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I take a lot of pills. I’ll need a list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get a full list at discharge. We’ll also send instructions to your pharmacy and dialysis center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you this afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue vancomycin during dialysis for six weeks. Get weekly labs—CBC, chem panel, and vancomycin levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who do I follow up with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nephrology, infectious disease, and your primary doctor. We’ll set those up before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my seizure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking oxcarbazepine and levetiracetam as before. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a lot of hospital stays. I just want to stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The key is staying on your meds, going to dialysis, and watching for fever or line issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Someone will help you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable, you’re afebrile, and your new line is working. You’re cleared to go home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll follow up like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Call us if you develop fever, chills, or any issues with the line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I watch for swelling or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your heart condition. If you have trouble breathing or sudden swelling, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well this admission. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take my vancomycin every dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s key to preventing another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the weekly labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the dialysis center will draw them and fax to infectious disease. Don’t skip those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. I want this to be the last hospital stay for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll see you around—hopefully not here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ha, same here. Take care and stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with fever and hypotension following a dialysis session, suspected to be due to a persistent infection of his tunneled femoral dialysis line. He was transferred from the ED to the ICU, started on vancomycin and gentamicin, and placed on vasopressor support. The infected line was removed on hospital day 2, and cultures confirmed MRSA bacteremia. After line removal, his blood pressure stabilized, vasopressors were weaned, and he completed a 'line holiday' while receiving IV vancomycin. A new tunneled dialysis catheter was successfully placed via the left external jugular vein on day 7. He remained afebrile with negative repeat blood cultures, and his heart function was reassessed with a TTE showing mild worsening. He was discharged home with services to continue six weeks of IV vancomycin during dialysis, with close monitoring of labs and follow-up with nephrology, infectious disease, and primary care.
